speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Would the minister comment on the report concerning indications of control stiffness in the CF-100, and will he inform the house whether to his knowledge this problem has been the cause of any crashes involving the type of aircraft in question?
Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National
Defence): About ten days ago there was some evidence shown in certain CF-100 planes that stiffness of the controls had developed under certain conditions of climate and temperature, and as a precautionary measure, while maintaining air defence operations, we did cut down training flights to a minimum in the interests of safety.
The matter has been under investigation by R.C.A.F. personnel and by officials of the Avro company, and I understand some progress has been made in dealing with the situation. So far as we know the weakness which did display itself on a few occasions has not been the cause of any crashes, although that is very difficult to say with certainty. It is not an extremely serious matter, and I expect that a solution will be found within a few days.

Would the minister say whether or not representations have been received by him or other members of the cabinet in opposition to the bill? Hon. V/. E. Harris (Minisier of Finance):
Mr. Speaker, may I answer with respect to the procedural part of the question.

Representations have been received this morning, not in opposition to the bill but suggesting certain amendments which might carry out more effectually the purpose of the bill, and those suggestions are to be followed by more direct reference to what is desired. Just before we came into the house I gave the assurance that until we had received the particular representations the bill would not be called or, at any rate, not passed. On the other point I have no answer to make because I have received no objections to the bill. As soon as I have received the representations I have mentioned, we shall consider them to see whether or not the bill ought to be delayed, or whether the proposed amendments coming forward could be put in the bill in the normal course at the committee stage.

Mr. Chairman, when we were last discussing clause 2 there were a number of features in the clause which came under consideration. I should like to say a further word about one of the matters, and what I wish to say is by way of comment on a statement made by the minister.
We have contended that this legislation, which provides for a sharing of hospital costs between the federal and provincial levels of government, should include the hospitalization of patients in tuberculosis hospitals and hospitals for the mentally ill. One of the arguments used by the minister in opposing our contention that there should be this extension is contained in a sentence or two to be found on page 3122 of Hansard for April 4, 1957. At that point the Minister of National Health and Welfare said:
We are simply following the pattern that exists in the province of Saskatchewan where tubercular patients and mentally ill patients are not covered by the hospital insurance scheme which, as my hon. friend knows, is basically on premium; but tney are covered under a separate account for tubercular people and mentally ill people.
The minister went on to say that the same practice is observed in British Columbia, and so on. It seems to me that the minister is distorting the picture when he tries to take the position that the federal government is following the pattern established in a province such as Saskatchewan. It is true that in Saskatchewan there are two separate accounts. Those in tuberculosis hospitals and in hospitals for the mentally ill are paid for out of general account, whereas hospitalization in general hospitals is paid for out of a special account which is set up on an insurance basis including the payment of premiums.
The over-all fact is that in the province of Saskatchewan-and it is true in the province of British Columbia as well-any person who requires to go to hospital, whether it be a general hospital on the one hand or a tuberculosis or mental hospital on the other, has his hospitalization covered. We suggest that is the basic fact, namely that in the provinces to which the minister has referred all types of hospitalization for whatever disease are covered under provincial arrangements.

Health Insurance
The federal government is now proposing at long last to get into this field and to share in the cost of hospitalization. But the federal government proposes to share only in that portion of hospitalization which relates to hospitalization in general hospitals. In my view the minister cannot put forward the argument about the insurance principle because, so far as the federal payment is concerned, he has already asserted-in fact he has boasted of it-that the federal payment is to come out of general revenue. There is not to be imposed by the federal government any premium for the purpose of collecting the money that Ottawa will pay into this hospitalization scheme. The federal money comes out of general account in the same way that the payment for tuberculosis patients and the payment for mental patients in the provinces of Saskatchewan and British Columbia come out of the general funds of the provinces.
If the minister wants to use other arguments as to why the federal government does not wish to come into this scheme he is free to do so, but I suggest that it is not fair for him to say that the federal government is following the Saskatchewan pattern. The Saskatchewan pattern is for the state, as represented by the province, to provide hospitalization for patients in all hospitals whatever the nature of the disease. The pattern in this legislation is for the federal government to provide hospitalization only for those who are in general hospitals. It excludes those in tuberculosis hospitals and in hospitals for the mentally ill.

Mr. Chairman, I object very strongly to subclause 2 of clause 6 being in this legislation at all. This is the subclause that requires the agreement of six provinces. I register my objection on two counts. In the first place I object to it from the point of view of law, if I can get into that field without running certain risks. It does seem to me that this is a case of giving to certain other jurisdictions the power of veto over legislation of this sovereign parliament.
By virtue of the British North America Act, when a bill has been passed by the House of Commons and the Senate and has received royal assent it is the law of the land. Yet by virtue of clause 6, subclause 2, we give to provincial legislatures the power, by failing to act, to veto this legislation and keep it from coming into force. As I said earlier, I concede the right of the government to say it will not bring in legislation until certain conditions have been met, but I object very strongly to conditions of this kind being written into a statute of the parliament of Canada.
We can pass this bill in the House of Commons, as I hope we will today. It can be passed in the other place and can be given royal assent before parliament is prorogued. It can even be proclaimed under the provisions of a later clause in the bill. Yet it can remain on the statute books of the Dominion of Canada without ever coming into actual effect because of the right of veto written right into this clause.
The other count on which I object to subclause 2 of clause 6 is that I think it is a ridiculously unreasonable requirement to continue to insist that there be at least six provinces agreeing to the legislation before it comes into effect. As I have pointed out

now on several occasions, the five provinces which have agreed contain within their boundaries 56.3 per cent of the entire population of Canada, and when I say "entire population of Canada" I draw attention to the fact that that percentage is based on the population of the ten provinces together with the population of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
As I have already pointed out, if the province of Prince Edward Island were to reach agreement with the federal government on this matter, technically the government's formula would be met. We would then have six provinces. But what would be the change in the population percentage? It would go up from 56.3 per cent to 56.9 per cent.

On clause 8-Dividends received by corporation.

The minister gave an explanation of this clause the other day, but I would like to ask him one question with respect to subsection (c). I quote the reference to the receiving corporation having acquired control of the payer corporation by the purchase from the corporation to which they were or have become subsidiary of shares of the capital stock of the payer corporation for a consideration not exceeding:
(c) in the case of shares that have a par value, the par value thereof,
Why is that provision necessary? Might it not in some cases be quite artificial? It might not represent the true value, and why should it be the par value?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am informed that the reason is to avoid any subsequent capital loss upon payment of dividends.

I am thinking of a company which possibly has one class of stock which has a par value and which also has an earned surplus. Would it not be reasonable to pay something more than the actual par value for the purchases of these shares?
Could I amplify that question. Surely there would be other ways of preventing the contingency to which the minister referred from arising.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will appreciate that this is quite complicated.
I do, and that is why I wanted it left over the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am informed that if you had paid-up capital stock and a surplus, that by the payment of a tax-free dividend you would in fact have a capital loss, and the purpose is to avoid that situation.

I am trying to get that through my head. As the minister says, it is a rather complicated section. He says that by the payment of a tax-free dividend you could get rid of the capital surplus, but need that payment take place prior to the purchase of the shares? The whole provision has to do with two parent companies amalgamating or merging, as I understand it. Well, then, if one of those companies has an earned surplus and happens to have only one class of stock with a par value, why should the purchasing company not be permitted to pay more than par on the purchase of the stock of the company which they are buying?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am also informed, in this particular instance at any rate, that since the purchase takes the form of the acquisition of shares in the company, the company being purchased then has shares in the purchasing company, the shareholders of that company-
Would you mind repeating that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Let us start with the company which is purchasing the other; the consideration is shares in the purchasing company.
That being the case, the transaction is not one which would prevent the payment of a reasonable price for the shares. On the other hand, if you were to allow the payment of a greater sum than the par value you would, as I have said a moment ago, permit the payment of the dividend tax-free, which would then put us in the position of having a capital loss, and we do not want to end up with that for tax reasons.

As I understand this section it has to do with the abolition of double

taxation on dividends. I just do not understand how this applies when there is a tax dividend and, as a consequence, a capital loss. It may be that I did not understand the original explanation, but it seemed very simple last Friday when the minister made it on the floor of the house. Possibly he did not himself know it too well at that time.

I am going to confess, quite frankly, that this is a complicated matter. There is an old jingle which comes to my mind. I do not know whether it is quite applicable to this situation, but mutatis mutandis it may be:
O what a tangled web we weave When first we practise to deceive.
There is no deception here, but it seems to me that here we may be weaving a very tangled web by introducing a consideration which seems artificial and unnatural. Why cannot nature take its course, so to speak? Why do we have to say things are different from what they are? Why fix an arbitrary value when the real value could be introduced? I have a feeling that we shall make this thing so complicated that a year or two from now something will have come up which nobody could have foreseen, with the result that we shall have to pass another complicated piece of legislation in order to undo what has been done here. Are we sure that nature could not be allowed to take its course?

On clause 9 there are really two parts of the amendment. The first adds to the present definition of earned income, and my question does not concern this part
Income Tax Act
of the amendment. But I am very concerned with the second part, the effect of which is to permit the deduction of certain items in the calculation of what would otherwise be earned income.
Hitherto, Mr. Chairman, the deductions which are now proposed in subclauses (d) and (e) were not deductible in arriving at the calculation of earned income, and the explanation given in the bill for permitting the deduction of these items is anything but satisfactory. We know, Mr. Chairman, that it is proposed that the taxpayer be permitted in arriving at his earned income to deduct two things, first, business losses sustained in the taxation year in the course of carrying on a business, and amounts taxable under section 79B in computing income for the taxation year.
As to section 79B, to which we shall be coming shortly, I think its inclusion is clear enough as a new section, pertaining to registered retirement savings plans. But I am much concerned as to the effect of subclause (d) which will permit a taxpayer for the first time, in calculating earned income, to deduct business losses. There is in the act no definition of business losses, and this phrase cannot mean expenses incurred in the course of earning an income. There would be no reason for having this clause in the bill at all if that were all it meant, because the act makes specific provision already, in arriving at net income, for a deduction of the expenses necessarily incurred in earning a particular income.
So what does this phrase mean, losses sustained in the taxation year in the course of carrying on a business? As I say, it obviously does not mean the expense incurred in the course of earning an income from that particular source, because in that case it would be totally unnecessary to introduce such a provision; it is contained in the act already.
It must, therefore, mean, on a proper interpretation, something very different from that kind of expense. What, then, can it mean? I am sure if this goes before a court it might well be interpreted as meaning capital losses. What are possible losses in business, in the absence of any definition in the act? There is a provision in section 12 (1) (b) of the act that in computing income no deduction will be allowed in respect of:
-an outlay, loss or replacement ol capital, a payment on account of capital or an allowance in respect of depreciation, obsolescence or depletion except as expressly permitted.
Here, however, you are introducing a provision which on the face of it looks like a contrary provision, the sort of thing for

Income Tax Act
which an exception is created under the provisions of section 12 (1) (b) of the act. Now, if the intention is to permit the deduction of business losses of a capital nature, then I think it is necessary to have a very close look at the situation here to see what is the proposed justification for this amendment, because if the minister is proposing that capital losses in business should be permitted in a situation of this kind, then I think the house should be well aware that it is introducing something that could have a very wide effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, no change has been made in the administration of law by this amendment. It is, in fact, a statement of what is being done at the present time.

It may be intended to be simply a codification of the existing practice, and if that were all one would not be raising any objection. "Business losses"-if the intention is simply to confine these to losses sustained in the carrying on of one business, why cannot we have that set out in terms clearer then these? "Business losses" is surely going to be interpreted by some tribunal- the income tax appeal board or the exchequer court or the Supreme Court of Canada-as including capital losses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it may be that one could use another phrase to describe what is intended, but I find, that this phrase is used in section 27 where we find the words "business losses sustained in the five taxation years immediately", and so on and so on. That is why the phrase is used in that manner, because it is a phrase known to the act at the present time and, as I said before and as my hon. friend accepts, it is intended strictly to be a definition of what is being done at the present time.
Once again I repeat, as I did on the former occasion, that if experience indicates that this has some result we did not foresee, then certainly someone will bring it before the house, either the Minister of Finance or perhaps an opposition member. But we do not foresee any more than the usual amount of trouble in applying the law when we make it.

The trouble with that kind of explanation is that these matters do not arise until after some taxpayer has been through the mill. The time comes to make an assessment, and in the face of the language of the act the officials of the department feel that they must proceed on such a course and the assessment is made. But when the remedial legislation is introducd, nobody thinks of going back and removing the assessment on the taxpayer who has been the victim of this severe interpretation.

speechtext:
Section 2 of the Income Tax Act reads as follows:
An income tax shall be paid . . . upon the taxable income for each taxation year of every person resident in Canada at any time in the year.
I realize that there are certain rules about residence, but the phrase, "person resident in Canada at any time in the year", occurs in section 2, which I have read and which is the general charging section. In addition, as my hon. friend points out, it also appears in section 38 of the act that we are now amending, and since the amendment does not relate to that particular matter the wording is left precisely as it is with the phrase "at any time."

What is to be the meaning? The minister has made reference to section 2, subsection 1, of the act. There are also the provisions of section 139, subsection 3, which define, for the purposes of the act, a person resident in Canada in a taxation year. He is such if (a) he sojourns in Canada in the year for a period in the aggregate of 183 days or more or (b) he was a member of the armed forces or (c) he was a member in general, let us say, of the civil service, the diplomatic corps, etc.
But it is this expression "at any time." We know what the act intends in the definition of a taxpayer resident in Canada. It eliminates the man who is just here on a temporary sojourn. You have specific rules in section 139 to determine what is to be residence in a year. But here-and it is admitted it is already in the section-you have the expression "at any time", which suggests that you are taking something away from the meaning of "residence" as determined by section 139, subsection 3.
Income Tax Act
Let us take a simple case. Section 38 of the act gives a very valuable benefit to persons who are in receipt of income in the form of dividends from Canadian corporations. It is a very valuable privilege in the hands of a taxpayer who has income of that nature. Here we have the provision extended to anyone who was resident in Canada at any time in the taxation year. I think we need a very clear statement as to the effect of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My understanding is that any person who is a resident of Canada pays an income tax if he comes within the terms of the act. In the section to which my hon. friend refers there is a statement that a person who is in Canada for a period of more than 183 days, or whatever it may be, is a resident. This does not mean that all persons who are not within that class are not residents. It is a statement that persons who are here that long undoubtedly are residents for the purpose of taxation.
But the problem is whether the person is a resident. If he is a resident, if he takes up residence, then he becomes subject to taxation. Therefore, as I understand it, it is not essential that one show that this person was physically within Canada for 183 days. It is only necessary to show that he is resident in Canada.
For that reason we have the two groups, one the person who is ordinarily resident, if I may use that phrase and, second, those who may be in here for a period of time beyond that mentioned in section 139 and therefore become subject to tax even if they may possibly claim that they are not residents. Hence we are not importing anything new here. In fact, we are repeating the words in the existing section. Once again it is remedial; that is to say, in the amendment before us we are doing what I think has been advocated by my hon. friend on other occasions and are preserving, if you will, the language of the section in every other respect except the proposed amendment.

Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue can tell us whether his department is experiencing any difficulty over the definition of "resident" in the case of persons who are not in Canada 183 days in the particular year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: If my hon. friend will address that question to the Minister of Finance who has the deputy minister before him he will give him an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am informed that there is no particular trouble. I am also referred to another section in the act which uses the same phrase.

Income Tax Act

Oh, yes; there are places
where the expression appears.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
There is no question about that. But we have not a definition here in the act apart from the definition in section 139, and it seems to be intended to be overridden by the expression used here.

I do not want to get involved in any technical explanations but how much content is there in the word "resident", an individual who is resident in Canada at any time? Does that mean that someone who is here casually can get this substantial benefit which ordinarily would go just to a Canadian resident on the strict basis of 183 days, or does the word "resident" itself import a substantial consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have sat here through a good many discussions on the Income Tax Act. I realize that these matters only come up when they occur to hon. members-and I do not recall any debate in the house prior to this time on the use of this phrase. That would lead me to think that the deputy minister is correct when he tells me there has been no trouble in administering the act using this phrase. Had there been any trouble, I am sure we would have heard of it, both from him and from the members of the committee. I do not see how there can be any conflict between the use of the word "resident" and resident at any time in the taxation year except that I suppose fom the standpoint of the draftsmen they repeat words which have been interpreted to mean something and they feel safer in continuing them from year to year until they find that they are not useful and then discard them. While I do not expect that I will ever be a draftsman, I would take the same view. I would not have brought forward the proposed amendment and changed words which it was unnecessary to change. I would only change those words that I felt would bring about the change I had in mind.

Having done that, I found that there were a great many side issues that must be considered as well and I was not able to complete that consideration by the time I brought in the budget recommendations. Nor would I want this to be taken as an indication that I thought we would be able to do so any time in the near future, although it does come to my mind immediately when we increase the $750 to $950 that it might be asked, "Why do you not carry on from $250 or whatever it may be to any sum higher than that?" Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) will recall that last week, during the discussion of the measure, he stated that he would tell the house on third reading what had been decided about this question of

relieving the construction workers who are obliged to leave their homes from tax on allowances made to them for board and lodging. Is he in a position to do that now?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. If the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I apologize for detaining the house at this time. However, the minister knows I never detain the house without justification. I intended to say a word or two on a point that concerns a number of my constituents but was called out hurriedly twice at inappropriate moments. That is the reason I am raising the matter at this time. The matter I wish to raise concerns a number of miners, smelter men and lumber men in my constituency and, I presume, in other constituencies across Canada. I refer to the question of loss occasioned men-workers particularly-who h,ave been resident in mining, lumbering or smelting camps for a number of years, long enough to erect residences or homes and to have an investment in those homes. I refer to the loss occasioned by the ceasing of operations which in effect not only means the loss of jobs but the loss of their investment in their homes, often savings over a long period of time: because as the operation concerned in most areas is permanently shut down it means that the investment in the home is reduced to almost nothing. I mention this matter because the companies concerned can, I understand, make deductions out of taxation from year to year for the cost of the homes provided for employees or bunk houses or staff houses and things of that sort. I understand that, according to the act, they are considered an operating cost and have always been permitted as a tax allowance.
I raise this question briefly because I believe an injustice is being done. I believe the workmen in these communities should receive the same consideration as the companies concerned. They suffer as individuals to a much greater extent from the loss of their savings and their homes and things of that sort. I do urge that this question be given consideration. I understand that some companies have obtained tax allowance for houses that were built for their employees and later purchased by the employees. In some cases these companies have made some allowance to compensate for the loss occasioned by the closing down of the camp, but that is not the same thing as having the workers treated in the same way as the companies concerned. I urge that consideration be given to what appears to me a grave injustice caused by the provisions of the act now.
Income Tax Act

I do not
intend to take more than a moment, sir, but the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) just asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) a question concerning whether or not travel expenses, board and lodging for people who are away from their normal place of work, should be included as income for purposes of taxation. I have a resolution on the order paper to this effect, but it will not be reached this session.
In view of the fact employees of the Department of National Revenue and the unemployment insurance commission receive allowances when they are away from their ordinary place of employment which are not included as income for taxation purposes, I do not understand why, to use an old expression, what is sauce for the goose is not sauce for the gander. I do not understand why one group of employees should not be taxed and another group should. I certainly have no objection to the employees of the Department of National Revenue or the unemployment insurance commission not having these expenses included as income for tax purposes; I think it is a very good idea. If this provision applies to employees of the government I certainly believe it should apply to other persons as well. This has been a source of considerable annoyance and a cause of concern to a number of people, particularly to organized labour, and I feel they have a justifiable complaint. I hope the minister will have some interesting information for us on this point when he closes the debate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) to give consideration to one other point which I shall state quite briefly. It has been drawn to my attention several times over the years, but it was drawn rather forcibly to my attention by a taxpayer just a few days ago.
The Income Tax Act, in section 27, does seem, for the purpose of deductibility with respect to charitable donations, to limit those donations to those made to charitable organizations to Canada. Those are the words in section 27 of the Income Tax Act. However, the income tax form which is placed in the hands of the taxpayers, and I hold in my hand a copy of the 1956 T-l form, does not indicate that that limitation applies. The words, in part read:
Charitable donations. A deduction for charitable donations is only allowable when the donations have been made to charitable organizations and are evidenced by proper receipts issued by those organizations and attached to your return.

Income Tax Act
My point is that there is nothing on the income tax form to indicate that it is only to organizations in Canada that contributions can be made and deductibility claimed. The most recent case drawn to my attention was that of a taxpayer who made contributions to funds for famine relief in India, and things of that sort, but the organizations to which he contributed had their head offices in the United States. My friend, who has been in touch with me, tells me that on one or two former occasions he had claimed deductions for similar items and they were allowed. This year the same types of claims were disallowed. Despite the generality of the language on the income tax form, there is the limitation in the act. I am not going to take the time now to make the argument that the act should be changed, as I believe it should, but certainly if there is this limitation it should be made clear on the forms placed in the hands of the taxpayers.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Just to clear up the last point first-I have nine minutes before I have to leave-may I say there is no question about the law as contained in section 27 of the Income Tax Act. Those donations are donations within Canada. It is true that the form does not disclose that, but the receipts themselves would disclose it. It may well be that on occasions those receipts were not checked in the manner in which they have been more recently. I am sure the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) will take into account what has been said with respect to the filing of receipts in future years. It may be that the form ought to be altered accordingly.
Now, to answer the requests of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) I may say the situation is this. The bulletin which was sent out last July 10 relating to the charging of these things is not, as we made clear, new law at all because charges for board and lodging have been provided for in the act for a number of years. I have been informed, in so far as administration is concerned, that it is not the intention to apply the bulletin to the year 1956, though some employers, and I think quite properly, began deductions upon receipt of the bulletin. If that is the case, there will be a refund, or a possible refund in some cases. It will apply to the taxation year 1957.
I made it quite clear that we felt we were providing for an interpretation of the law, as we understood it to be, and that we were

continuing to study the taxation of a great many allied subjects and fringe benefits, not for the purpose of adding to the tax but for the purpose of finding a logical explanation, if we could, for where we would draw the line. I am not prepared to recommend that the words "board and lodging" be taken out of the act. Indeed I do not think they should be. I did, however, make it clear that the construction industry seems to have been in the unique position of not having this tax apply to it over quite a period of time. I have not been able to determine whether this was because of the peculiar nature of the contractual relationship or the peculiar manner of recruiting construction workers for distant points. I cannot give my hon. friend any further assurance than I have, namely that the bulletin will not be used in a retroactive sense; but I do give the further assurance that we shall continue to look at this, having in mind the fact that construction projects of benefit to Canada in distant parts ought to go forward and if there is any impediment as a result of the tax laws which prevent development in Canada I do not think the house would expect us to maintain the impediment.

the second reading of Bill No. 403, to amend the Agricultural Products Marketing Act.
He	said:	The Agricultural Products
Marketing Act was passed in 1949; it came before this house as a result of a fairly long series of discussions which started in 1938.	The province of British Columbia
had over a considerable period been experimenting with legislation which provided for the setting up of marketing boards and they introduced legislation into their house on one or two occasions, which legislation was carried through to the privy council and declared to be ultra vires. Then, in 1934, they did bring in legislation which was carried to the privy council at that time and declared to be intra vires. At the same time they presented to the privy council an act which if passed by this parliament would pass on to provincial boards authority which could be given only by the federal legislation. When they presented this to us in 1938 we

asked for some further consideration having regard to the fact that probably more provinces should have taken advantage of the opportunity to set up boards than had done so up to that time before we should take action. They came back in 1939, just after we had embarked upon the war, and represented their requests with the suggestion that some other provinces had passed legislation making possible the setting up of boards. We indicated at that time that since we were entering upon wartime activities it would be necessary for the federal government to take over many of the authority which was then, in peacetime, with the provinces and we would be obliged to exercise during the time of war the authority we had under the War Measures Act. We said that therefore we did not think that was a suitable time to bring in the legislation which has come to be known eventually as Bill No. 82. So the farm organizations and those interested in boards of this kind and in legislation of this kind did not persist with the request that we have this legislation passed; they simply went on organizing in the provinces until the war was over. After the war they came back again each year to indicate most of the provincial legislations had provided for boards and asking for this special legislation.
In 1949 we answered those requests by bringing in what was called Bill No. 82 and that bill was described in the short title as the Agricultural Products Marketing Act, 1949. Now we have been carrying on with this legislation, assisting provincial marketing boards of one kind or another, and most of them have asked for whatever authority was required under this act, which authority has been granted from time to time. Therefore they were going along, with an act which met most of the conditions that were required, until the province of Ontario organized some marketing boards, to which they gave authority that was not anticipated in the earlier period.
I think the outstanding authority which they desired to have, and which the court eventually decided they did not have under provincial legislation, was to levy certain fees against those who were delivering to marketing boards and to utilize at least part of those fees for the purpose of equalizing payments or effecting the payments which were made to the farmers who entered into the marketing organization that was set up under the act. A few years ago a delegation came to the members of the government, particularly to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and myself and discussed whether or not we were prepared to pass legislation which would give the further authority 82715-206

Agricultural Products Marketing Act which the government of the province of Ontario and some of the farm organizations at least, if not all of them, desired should be given. We suggested at that time that if they would go as far as they thought they should go or desired to go in the passing of legislation, then, if the passing of the legislation was questioned and taken to the courts, and if they would wait until the courts had given their decision, we would then consider whether or not the legislation could be passed.
That program has been carried out; the Ontario legislature did pass legislation which they thought they should have and it was contested in the courts, or at least action was commenced in the courts. We suggested to them that the matter should be carried through the courts at that time. And in order to expedite that, we assisted them to get a stated case under the act before the court, and the court, as hon. members know, came to a decision just before the house met for this present session.
The legislation now before the house as an amendment is intended to meet the request which has been made, and I would just like to say in connection with it that the recommendation which was made by my department to the council and which has been put in the form of the bill now before the house recommended that the Agricultural Products Marketing Act be amended in such a way as to facilitate the prosecution of offenders under the act and to provide that marketing boards may collect fees and levies and use the funds thus obtained for the equalization of returns. The proposed amendments arise out of the recent judgment of the supreme court in respect to the farm products marketing reference which has more clearly defined the respective spheres of authority existing under federal and provincial legislation.
Prosecutions under the existing law present a problem where it is difficult to establish whether a product is to be marketed within a province or outside the province. One of the proposed amendments would place upon the accused the onus of proving that the product is not a regulated product within the meaning of the act. Further, it is proposed to make provision that where a prosecution is undertaken under a provincial act and it is found to be the federal act which is in fact contravened, the prosecution may proceed under the federal act notwithstanding that information has not been laid under such act. Both these amendments have been recommended by the attorney general of Ontario to bring the federal legislation in line with the Ontario legislation.
The proposed amendment relating to the collecting of fees and levies and the use of the

Agricultural Products Marketing Act funds thus raised for equalization of returns or pooling arises from the opinion of the supreme court that it is not within provincial authority to raise funds and use them in this way, as this constitutes indirect taxation. The authority to equalize returns through the use of funds and levies is, however, considered necessary to the success of certain marketing programs carried out by provincial marketing boards; that is, the authority to equalize returns through the use of fees is considered necessary by the provincial authorities. The amendment has been recommended to the government by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in its recent presentation and has been advocated very strongly by various organizations across the country. Mr. Speaker, with the general outline given by the minister I am in agreement, except that he did not go back to the original products marketing act which was placed on the statute books of this country in
1934	by the Bennett government. That act was known as the Natural Products Marketing Act. It covered most agricultural products, but in addition it contained clauses dealing with shingles and lumber, fruit and fruit products, maple products, tobacco, animals, meats, eggs, wool, dairy products, grains, seeds, vegetables and vegetable products, and other natural products of agriculture and of the forest, sea, lake or river.
That legislation was the first legislation placed on the statute books dealing with producers who were marketing their own products and in particular with the setting up of marketing boards, which have since become of very general importance and of general use. That legislation was based in the main upon certain legislation passed in British Columbia which was made applicable to the national field. It was opposed most strongly by the Liberal party when it was enacted, and up to the time it was enacted, and as soon as Mr. King was returned as Prime Minister in
1935	that legislation was submitted to the courts to determine whether or not it came within the legislative competence of parliament.


While the courts decided that it did not, it is of interest to know that in the recent submissions made with respect to the Agricultural Products Marketing Act many of the arguments which Mr. Bennett often stated should have been placed before the supreme court and the privy council, and which he contended would have caused those courts to come to the conclusion that the legislation was within the competence of parliament, were followed by the counsel who argued the case. As one looks back over a period of 22 years and finally arrives at the point where the Supreme Court of Canada in its majority judgment agrees with the contentions of Mr. Bennett, it is indeed of some interest to those of us who engage in the practise of law that so often we find that arguments unused on one occasion, when used many years afterwards may bring about a change in the judgment rendered.
As far as this legislation is concerned, the minister has set forth in general the course which has been followed with reference to this act. The degree to which farm marketing plans are in operation is not so generally known. Ontario today has 17 marketing plans covering 30 products to a value of $290 million. That shows the degree to which this type of legislation and the placing of the marketing of farm products in the hands of the producers to a great extent has advanced since 1934 when Mr. Bennett's government brought this legislation to which I referred before the house.
The largest scheme in Canada is, of course, Ontario's hog marketing co-operative with over 30,000 members and an annual sale exceeding $100 million.
All of the provinces but Newfoundland have marketing legislation today, although Alberta, Quebec and Nova Scotia have no marketing boards in existence. Ontario, with its vast marketing system and with the government of that province naturally interested in assuring that such legislation would be as effective and as beneficial as possible, suggested, and the federal government agreed therewith, the submission of certain questions to the Supreme Court of Canada with a view to determining the legislative jurisdiction in respect of these matters to which the minister made reference. The judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada is a long and complicated one but I think that in general the minister has summarized the effect of the majority judgments on the reference in question.
The conclusion was that the province of Ontario marketing legislation was within provincial jurisdiction but that boards established under it could not operate beyond Ontario's borders; that the province of

Ontario or any province lacked the necessary power to authorize levies to pay losses, to set up reserves or to provide equalization payments to producers. Such levies were declared to be a form of indirect taxation which, under the British North America Act, comes within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal parliament.
I have before me the recent amendments to the farm products marketing act of the province of Ontario which were passed at the last session of the legislature. The powers under that act are wide and most comprehensive. They grant to marketing boards in the province of Ontario the power to investigate, adjust or settle any dispute arising in connection with the producing, processing, distributing or transporting of any regulated product. These marketing boards also have the power to investigate prices and price spreads, to require all persons to register who are engaged in producing or marketing a regulated product. Full provision is made for the licensing of all those who will engage in these processes and provision is also made for the fixing of licence fees. Boards also have the power to fix and allot quotas and to require that the price payable or owing to the producers for the regulated product shall be paid to or through a local board. Provision is also made under the Ontario act for the making of regulations covering prices, grades, quantities, et cetera, that may be marketed by each producer, and also for the prosecution of any person who pays less than the minimum price as fixed by the board.
As the minister has stated, the amendments now before the house were requested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
I have here the submissions made by that organization in January of 1957, and I shall quote from them for I think they clarify the purposes of the legislation. They say:
Whereas marketing legislation aimed at enabling agricultural producers to develop orderly self-help production and marketing programs is now in effect in nine provinces of Canada;
Whereas the validity of certain provincial marketing legislation in effect in Ontario is being challenged . . .
Whereas provincial and federal governments have severally and individually jurisdictional authority over these matters;
Resolved that the provincial governments be requested to continue to actively support effective producer marketing legislation, and in co-operation with the federal authorities develop complementary legislation which will permit the orderly marketing of farm products.
In their presentation to the cabinet on February 15, 1957, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture also made this submission:
Based on the Supreme Court of Canada decision . . . further federal legislation is needed if producer boards are to be enabled to carry on certain 82715-206J

Agricultural Products Marketing Act functions which they consider will often be essential to effective orderly marketing of farm products.
Those in general represent the presentations made by farmers. I have as well the presentation made by the president of the Ontario federation of agriculture in which he sets out the request made to the federal government for legislation similar to that now introduced by the minister.
We in the Progressive Conservative party believe that legislation of this kind, demanded as it is by farm organizations across Canada in the interests of orderly marketing, deserves and commands our support. We believe that on the basis of the record of farm marketing organizations this legislation, while it does mark an unusual step forward, is necessary. We believe that the powers contained in the legislation, being subject to a form of revocation by the governor in council, assure that in the application of the legislation the rights and equities of people in general will be preserved and maintained while at the same time assuring to the farmer and to those engaged in the production, processing and distribution of farm products fair and equitable treatment.
I think all of us can pay our tribute to the work that has been accomplished by the marketing boards that have existed. This is a form of self-help. Instead of asking governments to do for them, they themselves ask their governments for the opportunity to do for themselves.
I believe, however, that in addition to this legislation further action is necessary. In view of the fact that the Supreme Court of Canada has determined the distribution of powers between the federal and provincial governments we believe that the time has come when, in the interests of the national welfare of agriculture, a national conference on agriculture should be convened. This would be representative of the federal and provincial governments and of farm organizations with the responsibility of suggesting a general policy for domestic and international trade so as to assure the farmer a fair and proper share of the national income and also permit farmers to have a part in formulating policies for the promotion of the welfare of agriculture.
In saying that the opposition is giving its support to this legislation, I do say to the minister, however, that irrespective of the circumstances under which clause 3 of the bill has come into being I am of those who through the years have opposed legislation which places the onus upon an accused or defendant in a prosecution. The power possessed by the governor in council of revocation of any authority granted under one of the sections would appear to be one that will assure the preservation and maintenance of the public interest. At the same time the legislation in general will permit farmers and producers to extend and expand the field within which agriculture has attained its greatest advance, namely through producers by self-help making their contribution to their own prosperity rather than relying on the state to assure them a fair and proper return for the products which they produce. Any measure that has as its purpose self-help rather than making any organization a leaner on the state is, I believe, a step in the right direction, and one that deserves support.

The situation that caused this action on the part of the tree fruit growers of British Columbia was chaotic marketing. I refer to the unnecessary competition between the growers themselves in a limited market on the prairies-the export market had then not been developed to a great extent-and the robber barons engaged in the distribution of fruit in the prairie provinces at that time. The chaotic conditions caused by those two influences were the reason for the decision by the representatives of the tree fruits industry to study the matter. As a result of giving over a period of years some lengthy consideration to the question of what should be done in a legislative way to correct the situation, they finally recommended to the government of the day in British Columbia that marketing legislation of this type was necessary.
Getting the legislation through the legislature was a long job. There was opposition from various quarters. Finally a marketing bill was passed. Then it was challenged and its validity was ruled upon by the privy council and finally it was declared intra vires. I remember very well that, when the telegram was sent to all the members of the committee at various points in British Columbia informing them of the decision of the privy council there was general rejoicing at that fact.
The results have indicated and proved the good judgment of the fruit growers concerned at that time. I could give numerous illustrations. I make these few brief remarks because this type of legislation is strongly supported by members of this group. In fact it is one aspect of our agricultural policy and has been such throughout the years. In order to give one concrete illustration of how the farmer was protected by this legislation, may I say that prior to the marketing act of British Columbia being placed on the statute books of that province and prior to the establishment of the tree fruits board in that province, the average amount claimed per year by the robber barons on the prairies in the fruit business for cherries that were supposed to arrive in poor condition was 14 per cent. We have sent hundreds and thousands of crates through our packing houses, and inevitably we would get back from Calgary, Edmonton or some other point like that a telegram saying that

I mention that as a clear illustration of what can be done by farmers or fruit growers under the protection of satisfactory legislation. He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill has already been before the Senate and was referred to a committee of the Senate. It has been gone over rather carefully, and I do not think there were any suggestions that there be amendments made to it. I therefore will not go too far into detail in connection with it in moving the second reading of the bill; but I think probably I should make a short statement on it.
The present Fertilizers Act was enacted in 1922 and amended in 1927 and 1948. Its basic provisions are to require fertilizers sold in Canada to be marked to show their guaranteed plant food content of nitrogen, phosphorus and potash; to provide for sampling and analysis to ensure they meet their guarantees and to require them to be registered.
The present act continues a large number of details which are now inadequate or outdated in view of recent developments in the fertilizer trade and fertilizer usage. As illustrations, (a) it does not provide adequately for trace mineral elements, such as copper and boron which are now being introduced in fertilizer mixtures; (b) it requires that the phosphorus and potassium components of fertilizers be identified and analysed as phosphoric acid and potassium oxide; whereas the present trend is to identify and analyse them on an elemental basis as phosphorus and potassium-the present bill will allow for this adjustment when desirable; (c) the present act requires each fertilizer to be re-registered each year, but it is now considered that with respect to many fertilizers permanent registration could be granted, thereby lightening the administrative load both on the department and on the industry; (d) it specifies certain methods of sampling which are now at variance with established standard control methods.
For some years fertilizer users, as represented by provincial fertilizer boards and the fertilizer industry, have made representations to the department that the legislation should be amended to bring the above and other similar detailed requirements up to date. The
Fertilizers
bill before parliament at the present time in no way changes the basic provisions of the basic act. The major change is that Bill 400 provides for various details with respect to registration, composition, packaging, labelling, sampling and analyses to be established by regulation by the governor in council rather than under the act as it is at present. This is considered desirable, as it will permit the more ready amendment of those details as may be necessary to maintain them in keeping with changing conditions and practices in fertilizer usage.
The general structure of Bill 400 follows the pattern of agricultural legislation of this type brought to parliament in recent years.
In view of the fact that the bill has been gone over very carefully by a committee of the Senate and is recommended to this house, I do not think it is necessary at this moment to say anything further, but when we are considering the measure in committee these matters can be gone into further.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT CLARIFYING POSITION OF MEMBERS AS SERVANTS OF THE CROWN
speechtext: Is the minister going to explain the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT CLARIFYING POSITION OF MEMBERS AS SERVANTS OF THE CROWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the explanation of the bill is pretty largely covered by the explanatory note. Hon. members will recall that on a couple of occasions since I became minister we have brought in bills to extend the liability of the crown in actions between the crown and a subject with the result that now the crown is, I think, fully as liable to the subject in respect of any contracts or torts as the subject is responsible to another subject.
The purpose of the present bill is to maintain a liability which we have always recognized. In other words, we have always considered that members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, when they were going about the country in the discharge of their duties, should be regarded as servants of the crown so that if they commit any tort upon a subject we as their masters would be responsible to that subject for the full amount of the damages which their tort had inflicted.
Recently there was a decision of the privy council in a case that arose in New South Wales which raised a serious doubt whether members of a police force are servants within

the meaning of that legal principle. If we were to leave the law in Canada in the condition in which this privy council judgment may have left it, then we could perhaps have this result-indeed and I would think it more than likely-if someone who had been injured by a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, thinking that he could recover indemnity from the crown, sued the crown as the master and the principle of this judgment were applied, which holds that the crown is not the master of a policeman at law, then the subject in that case would not succeed in his claim against the crown.
The whole purpose of the present bill is to confirm the law in the position in which we have always admitted it to be, namely that the crown should continue to be liable to anyone who has been wrongfully injured by a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police while engaged in the discharge of his duties.

subtopic: AMENDMENT CLARIFYING POSITION OF MEMBERS AS SERVANTS OF THE CROWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, boiled down, I think the minister has stated the purpose of the bill, to bring the legal situation regarding police officers who perform their duties by virtue of their office into line with modern thinking. I think the common law distinguishes between the position of master and servant and that of a police officer and his employer. Under the Crown Liability Act passed a few years ago by parliament the crown was made subject to actions for damages caused by any civil servant while in the course of his employment, and the armed forces were later included. I take it that the minister and the government feel that the R.C.M.P. are in a little different position than the armed forces. Otherwise they would have been brought under the other act.
Apparently a doubt has been raised by the case of Attorney General for New South Wales v. Perpetual Trustee Company. I have not read the case but I take it that the decision does not put police officers in the same category as members of the armed services and that heretofore there has been a wrong interpretation of the position of members of the R.C.M.P.
I understand this is the sole purpose of bringing them into that relationship. In other words, by statute we simply make officers and men of the R.C.M.P. servants of the crown, so to speak. In other words, the crown will be liable for any damages caused by any of their acts while on duty in the course of their employment. It changes the old axiom in the common law in a sense because of modern thinking.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: That it is expedient that the houses of parliament approve the statute of the international atomic energy agency signed by Canada at New York on October 26, 1956, and that this house do approve the same.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: APPROVAL OF STATUTE OF INTERNATIONAL AGENCY
speechtext:
My colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests that I might make a preliminary statement. This resolution arises out of a proposal that was first made by the President of the United States to the general assembly of the United Nations in 1953. After his conference with the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the Prime Minister of France he went to the assembly of the United Nations and proposed that an effort be made to set up an agency to provide for the peaceful uses of atomic energy. It was particularly appropriate that that proposal should come from the President of the United States because, as the major atomic energy power, the invitation and the
Atomic Energy
suggestion made by the president bore all the earmarks of something that was both important and very reassuring.
As a result of the proposal which was made there was a meeting, I think some time in December, 1953. A negotiating group, of which Canada was a member, representing a number of atomic energy countries began negotiations in Washington with a view ultimately to the presentation of a statute which was to be accepted by the members of the United Nations and certain other member states not members of the United Nations. These negotiations between the eight powers continued until the fall of 1955 when a draft statute was placed before the general assembly for consideration. As a result of the consideration given by the general assembly it was decided to extend from eight to twelve the number of negotiating countries which brought in, amongst others, India. Then for a period of some months these 12 negotiating countries gave further consideration to the matter in Washington. Ultimately there was presented last September, not at the general assembly but at a meeting held at the United Nations, a draft statute to which some 87 countries gave their general adherence. This statute now awaits ratification by Canada and other nations.
Canada, I may say in speaking from recollection of the last series of meetings held at the United Nations, did play a notable part in the early negotiations in Washington and later at the United Nations prior to and during the presentation of the draft statute. The body set up by this general conference will have the character, for the purpose of administration, of a specialized agency of the United Nations, although it will not be in fact a specialized agency of the United Nations. It will be a body that will, from time to time under certain conditions, make reports to the United Nations. It will have its own board of governors, of whom five must come from the most advanced nations in the technology of atomic energy, including the production of source materials, and one other must come from North America, Latin America, western Europe, eastern Europe, Africa and the Middle East, south Asia, south-east Asia and the Pacific and the Far East.
The purpose of the organization is one which I am sure will commend itself to all hon. members. It represents an attempt to provide for the benefit of mankind the peaceful uses of atomic energy. It is with that in mind we are now asking the house to approve the statute of the atomic energy agency which we signed in New York on October 26, 1956. This will enable Canada to proceed with ratification so that Canada may

National Capital Plan
join other nations in making it possible for this important agency to come into being and serve the constructive interest of mankind.

subtopic: MEASURE TO CONSTITUTE NATIONAL CAPITAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I already indicated some days ago that it was not the government's intention to ask parliament to complete action this session on the measure which this resolution would precede. We felt, however, that it was desirable that hon. members of this house and those in the other place, who did such useful work on this subject last year in the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the federal district commission, should now have an opportunity to see the government's proposals in regard to the legislation while their recollections of the work they did is still relatively fresh in their minds.
It will be recalled that the joint committee, in part IV of their report, recommended that the Federal District Commission Act be revised. They noted that since the present act was drafted both Canada and the national capital have developed substantially, and they suggested it was appropriate that the act should be revised in order to bring the definition of the powers, the duties and the responsibilities of the commission in line with the development of the national capital area. They went on to recommend that the name of the act and of the commission be changed, and we are disposed to recommend that their recommendation be adopted by parliament.
This description of the area as the federal district commission was subject to some misinterpretation because of the fact that there are other federal district commissions which are separate from the usual city or territorial administration. The bill which has been prepared does not contemplate removing any part of the territory from the ordinary jurisdiction of the provincial authorities which have jurisdiction in respect of all municipal matters, and it was felt that it would be less ambiguous and less subject to misinterpretation if we merely called it the national capital area. That does not mean that it is not normally subject to the ordinary rules of municipal and provincial

administration, but that there is a commission that is giving special attention to the development of the area.
The committee also recommended that the chairman of the commission be employed full time in this office, and the bill which will follow the adoption of this resolution, if it is adopted, implements that to the extent that it makes it permissible to have that done. But after discussing it with the present chairman of the federal district commission, it was found that at the present time, and for perhaps the next several months or a year or two, it would not be necessary for the one who is at the head of the commission to devote the whole of his time to it and, as a matter of fact, the gentleman who is the chairman of the federal district commission is rendering very useful advisory service to the government of Alberta in connection with the eastern slopes of the Pacific; to the government of Ontario in connection with its legislation and regulations concerning the administration of the forest and water resources of the province; and he is also consulted by the government of Newfoundland as to the economic possibility of there being established new pulp and paper mills there that would not overtax the resources of the forests of that province, but would add to the economy of the province without endangering the future of the existing establishments or the establishments that might be made if it were found that the forest wealth would support additional establishments.
It was felt that that was something that was of value to the economy of the nation and the chairman, from his experience, told me that he thought he would like to devote something more than half his time to the work of the commission but he did not think that he would be working full time even if he were required to abandon the other retainers that he has from the government of Alberta, the government of Ontario and the government of Newfoundland.
The bill as drafted does provide that the chairman may be a full-time or a part-time chairman, and it would be our intention, if we are still responsible for the administration, to retain the present chairman of the commission on a part-time basis, with the understanding that he will-and I am sure he will-if he finds more time is required than he anticipates-he now anticipates that it would take something more than half his time but not the whole of his time because he is the very conscientious gentleman we know him to be-bring that to the attention of whoever was responsible to parliament as a liaison between parliament and the commis-
National Capital Plan
sion and suggest a different recommendation to parliament.
My attention has been drawn to the fact that it is six o'clock. May I interrupt at this moment and continue at eight o'clock the few remarks I have to make on the other portions of the resolution.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
